reference.source: Mulliken and Young's Vascular Anomalies: Hemangiomas and Malformations
clinicalPearls: Locally aggressive, borderline vascular tumour of infancy that infiltrates tissue planes but does not metastasise.
The principal tumour underlying the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon: severe thrombocytopenia with consumptive coagulopathy.
Presents as a firm, indurated, violaceous and warm plaque, commonly on the trunk, extremities or retroperitoneum.
GLUT1-negative with lymphatic endothelial (D2-40) positivity, sharing a spectrum with tufted angioma.
Somatic GNA14 mutations are reported in a subset of lesions.
Platelet transfusion should generally be avoided unless there is active bleeding, as it aggravates trapping and swelling.
Sirolimus (mTOR inhibitor), often combined with corticosteroids, is the mainstay of systemic therapy; vincristine is an alternative.
Retroperitoneal and intrathoracic lesions carry higher morbidity and mortality.
reference.pathophysiology: Kaposiform haemangioendothelioma is an infiltrative vascular neoplasm composed of coalescing lobules and sheets of spindled endothelial cells forming slit-like, crescentic vessels reminiscent of Kaposi sarcoma, intermingled with abnormal lymphatic channels (D2-40 positive) and microthrombi. The disorganised vasculature and abnormal endothelium trap and activate platelets, triggering intralesional platelet aggregation, profound thrombocytopenia and secondary consumptive coagulopathy, together termed the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon. Activating GNA14 mutations and dysregulated angiogenic and lymphangiogenic signalling drive growth, and mTOR pathway activity provides the rationale for sirolimus.
additionalInvestigations: Biopsy showing characteristic infiltrative spindled vascular lobules with D2-40 positivity
Full blood count demonstrating marked thrombocytopenia
Coagulation profile with low fibrinogen, raised D-dimer and prolonged clotting times
Contrast-enhanced MRI delineating an ill-defined infiltrative enhancing mass crossing tissue planes
Baseline and serial monitoring during sirolimus therapy
redFlags: Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon with profound thrombocytopenia and bleeding
reference.prognosis: Mortality can be significant when the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon complicates large or deep lesions, but sirolimus-based therapy has markedly improved outcomes. Residual fibrosis, chronic pain and lymphoedema may persist.
pitfalls: Routine platelet transfusion, which aggravates platelet trapping and lesion swelling.
Mistaking the coagulopathy for primary immune thrombocytopenia or sepsis.
Underestimating deep or visceral extent by relying on the surface appearance.
Delaying systemic therapy while awaiting spontaneous resolution.
references: Consensus guidance on management of kaposiform haemangioendothelioma and the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon
management: Give sirolimus as first-line systemic therapy, often with corticosteroids, especially when the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon is active
Support the consumptive coagulopathy with fibrinogen or cryoprecipitate and fresh frozen plasma
Avoid platelet transfusion unless there is active bleeding or planned surgery, as transfused platelets are trapped and may worsen swelling
Consider surgical resection for accessible, localised lesions
Undertake serial monitoring of platelet count, fibrinogen and D-dimer, with imaging and laboratory surveillance during sirolimus therapy
Manage residual pain, fibrosis and lymphoedema within a multidisciplinary vascular anomalies team
